children: Asian stocks fell, tracking losses on Wall Street, as surging oil prices stoked inflation concerns and as Treasury yields rose. Oil extended gains over $101 per barrel.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index slipped 0.3%, with benchmark gauges in Japan and Australia opening lower, while South Korea’s was little changed. The S&P 500 Index fell 0.5% in the US session, led by industrial and consumer-discretionary shares. The Nasdaq 100 Index dropped 0.3% as Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and Alphabet Inc. declined.

The 10-year Treasury yield was steady in Asian trading after rising Wednesday as the US government’s plan to buy up to $6 billion of longer-dated debt disappointed some investors who had expected a larger increase. West Texas Intermediate rose to around $97 a barrel early Thursday while Brent advanced 0.5% to $101.69 as escalating Middle East tensions raised concerns about energy supplies, adding to expectations the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates to contain inflation.

The combination of higher oil prices and rising bond yields leaves markets particularly sensitive to Friday’s US inflation report, which may determine whether the Fed raises rates this month. A stronger-than-expected reading may reinforce bets on further tightening and put additional pressure on stocks and bonds, while softer data could revive expectations that policymakers will remain on hold.
“The longer elevated prices persist, the harder it becomes for markets to shrug the inflation impulse,” said Evelyne Gomez-Liechti, a multi-asset strategist at Mizuho International Plc.

President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about oil prices and a war he said will end after the midterm election, though hostilities show little sign of easing. Iran will escalate its counterstrikes if the US continues attacking its territory and infrastructure, according to a senior official from the Islamic Republic.
“The temperature just got turned up again,” said Kenny Polcari at SlateStone Wealth. “The risk premium is alive and well, and the risk to energy supplies coming out of the Gulf is real.”

Bloomberg’s gauge of the dollar slipped for a fourth day Thursday. The yen was steady after advancing 0.3% the previous day as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged traders to test his resolve on supporting Japan’s currency.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release August producer-price data on Thursday, followed by the consumer-price-index numbers on Friday.
Swaps imply about a 62% chance the Fed will raise rates by a quarter point on Sept. 16, up from 60% on Tuesday. At least two hikes by the middle of next year are fully priced in.

“A hot CPI print would all but seal a September hike and underpin a firmer dollar,” said Elias Haddad at Brown Brothers Harriman & Co. “A cooler reading would strengthen the case for a hold and leave the dollar vulnerable to a dovish Fed repricing.”

title: Asian stocks fall as oil stokes inflation fears
